vision.statement: Understand Dyslexia is made for top-tier researchers offering a birds-eye view of the whole dyslexia research ecosystem and representing it simply via playful UX
vision.description: This section provides a comprehensive, research-backed overview of dyslexia across multiple domains - from definitions and etiology to brain structure, developmental trajectories, and theoretical models. The content is designed to be both scientifically rigorous and accessible, using interactive elements and visual metaphors to make complex research concepts engaging and understandable.
vision.audience: Researchers, educators, clinicians, and anyone seeking a deep, evidence-based understanding of dyslexia

sections.name: What is Dyslexia?
sections.description: Definitions, classifications, prevalence, and diagnostic criteria from 111 verified research claims

content.definition: Dyslexia is predominantly characterized by a core deficit in phonological processing (the ability to recognize and manipulate speech sounds), which results in impairments in decoding (sounding out words), spelling, and word recognition. It is a neurobiological in origin specific learning disability.
keyPoints: Neurobiological origin - brain-based, not due to lack of intelligence
Specific to reading and related language skills (word-level reading difficulties)
Characterized by persistent difficulties in accurate and/or fluent word recognition and spelling
Primary difficulties at the word-reading level with phonological awareness, decoding, encoding and/or oral reading fluency
Distinct from developmental language disorder (DLD) which affects language comprehension

prevalence.overview: Reading ability is continuously and normally distributed in the population, making prevalence estimates arbitrary based on chosen cutoff points.
prevalence.estimates: Commonly cited 5-10% or 7-15% of population, but this depends on diagnostic criteria
prevalence.continuumView: The continuum view leads to variations in dyslexic samples across studies in research contexts
prevalence.note: The 2025 IDA definition no longer references unexpectedness in relation to cognitive ability
prevalence.genderDistribution: Equal prevalence in males and females when using same diagnostic criteria
prevalence.crossLinguistic: Prevalence varies across languages and orthographies due to orthographic depth

definitionEvolution.traditional: Earlier definitions emphasized 'unexpected difficulty' in relation to cognitive ability
definitionEvolution.current2025: The 2025 International Dyslexia Association definition removes unexpectedness language and intellectual functioning as defining components
definitionEvolution.policy: The U.S. First Step Act (2018) still retains the unexpectedness framing
definitionEvolution.international: The UK Rose Report (2009) explicitly conceptualized dyslexia as a continuum with no clear cut-off points
definitionEvolution.implications: Definition changes affect policy, resource allocation, and educational practice

classification.title: Dyslexia Subtypes

accuracyDisabled.name: Accuracy-Disabled
accuracyDisabled.preschoolProfile: Deficits in phonological and morphological awareness but intact RAN

rateDisabled.name: Rate-Disabled
rateDisabled.preschoolProfile: Impaired RAN but preserved phonological and morphological awareness

classification.longitudinal: Research supports distinct subtypes with different developmental trajectories
classification.implications: Different subtypes may require different intervention approaches

diagnosticCriteria.title: Diagnostic Criteria
coreCriteria: Persistent difficulties with accurate and fluent word recognition
Difficulties are unexpected relative to other cognitive abilities
Difficulties are not better explained by other conditions
assessmentTools: Word reading and pseudoword reading tests
diagnosticCriteria.ageOfIdentification: Typically identified in early elementary school (ages 6-8), but can be identified earlier with screening

misconceptions.title: Common Misconceptions
misconceptions.intelligence: Myth: Dyslexia is caused by low intelligence. Reality: Dyslexia occurs across the full range of intellectual abilities.
misconceptions.vision: Myth: Dyslexia is a vision problem. Reality: Dyslexia is a language-based learning disability, not a visual processing disorder.
misconceptions.laziness: Myth: Children with dyslexia are lazy or not trying hard enough. Reality: Dyslexia is a neurobiological condition affecting reading ability.
misconceptions.outgrowth: Myth: Children will outgrow dyslexia. Reality: Dyslexia is a lifelong condition, but interventions can significantly improve reading skills.
misconceptions.gender: Myth: More boys than girls have dyslexia. Reality: Equal prevalence when using same diagnostic criteria; boys are more likely to be identified due to behavioral factors.

sections.name: Causes (Etiology)
sections.description: Genetic, neurological, cognitive, and environmental factors from 166 verified research claims

content.overview: The etiology of dyslexia is multifactorial, involving complex interactions between genetic predisposition, neurobiological differences, cognitive processing deficits, and environmental influences. Multiple interacting risk factors across domains contribute to different individual profiles.

heritability.estimates: Heritability estimates range from 40-80% based on twin and family studies
heritability.gwas: 2022 GWAS of 51,800 adults with dyslexia and 1,087,070 controls estimated SNP-based heritability at h²SNP=0.152 (5% prevalence) and h²SNP=0.189 (10% prevalence)
heritability.sexCorrelation: Genetic correlation between males and females for dyslexia was 0.91, indicating similar genetic etiology between sexes

keyGenes.overview: 42 independent genome-wide significant loci identified in 2022 GWAS
keyGenes.cognitive: 15 loci in genes linked to cognitive ability/educational attainment
keyGenes.specific: 27 new loci potentially more specific to dyslexia

geneEnvironment.overview: Genetic predisposition interacts with environmental factors
geneEnvironment.ses: Low socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with higher probability of dyslexia and exacerbates genetic contribution
geneEnvironment.parental: Parental education moderates the effect of genetic risk variants on reading ability
geneEnvironment.pollutants: Environmental pollutants may selectively target dyslexia-related genes

grayMatter.overview: Differences in gray matter volume in reading-associated regions
regions: Left occipito-temporal cortex (including visual word form area)
grayMatter.note: Replication of these findings has been inconsistent

regions: Arcuate fasciculus (reduced fractional anisotropy in some studies)
whiteMatter.genetic: READ1 deletion in DCDC2 gene associated with lower global efficiency in white matter networks

patterns: Hypoactivation in left hemisphere reading networks (occipito-temporal, temporoparietal, inferior frontal)
Compensatory hyperactivation in right hemisphere homologues in some individuals
Altered functional connectivity during reading tasks

neuralTiming.overview: Evidence for deficits in neural entrainment and temporal processing
neuralTiming.networks: Particularly in auditory and speech processing networks

classification.accuracy: Classification accuracy of 65-90% in controlled cohorts
classification.caution: Limited generalizability to real-world populations, not for clinical diagnostic use

cognitive.overview: Multiple cognitive factors contribute to dyslexia

evidence: Phonological awareness deficits across languages and orthographies
Phonological processing impairments predict reading difficulties
Evident in both children and adults with dyslexia

doubleDeficit.evidence: Distinct subtypes with single and double deficits supported by research

ran.overview: Rapid Automatized Naming (RAN) deficits consistently observed
evidence: RAN speed correlates with reading fluency
RAN deficits persist even when phonological awareness is intact
RAN and phonological awareness contribute independently to reading ability

workingMemory.overview: Mixed evidence for working memory deficits
findings: Some studies show verbal working memory impairments
Other studies find deficits only when phonological processing demands are high
May be secondary to phonological processing difficulties
Slower naming speed (RAN) is a robust finding
General processing speed deficits are less consistent
May be domain-specific rather than general

attention.overview: Evidence for attention deficits is mixed
findings: Some studies report attention control difficulties
Others find attention deficits only in comorbid ADHD
Not considered a core feature of dyslexia

environmental.overview: Environmental factors significantly affect dyslexia risk and outcomes

ses.overview: Socioeconomic status consistently affects dyslexia risk
effects: Low SES associated with higher prevalence of reading difficulties
SES moderates genetic risk - low SES exacerbates genetic contribution
SES affects access to early intervention and educational resources

factors: Prenatal exposure to environmental pollutants linked to dyslexia risk
Preterm birth and low birth weight associated with increased risk
Prenatal nutrition may play a role (evidence emerging)

educational.overview: Educational quality and instruction affect outcomes
factors: Quality of reading instruction moderates expression of dyslexia
Early identification and intervention improve outcomes

sections.name: Brain & Neurology
sections.description: Brain structure, function, connectivity, and plasticity from Phase 2 neurological research

content.overview: Research has identified patterns in brain structure and function associated with dyslexia, but individual differences are significant. The brain remains plastic throughout life, meaning that intervention can be effective at any age. Neuroimaging findings show both structural and functional differences, though replication varies.

grayMatter.title: Gray Matter Differences
grayMatter.overview: Studies have reported differences in gray matter volume in regions associated with reading

leftOccipitoTemporal.name: Left Occipito-Temporal Cortex
leftOccipitoTemporal.function: Includes the visual word form area for rapid word recognition
leftOccipitoTemporal.location: Back of the brain, near visual processing areas
leftOccipitoTemporal.findings: Differences reported, but replication has been inconsistent
leftOccipitoTemporal.significance: Critical for developing reading expertise and automatic word recognition

inferiorFrontal.name: Inferior Frontal Gyrus
inferiorFrontal.function: Involved in phonological processing and reading
inferiorFrontal.findings: Structural differences observed in some studies
inferiorFrontal.significance: Important for articulation, speech production, and phonological working memory

temporoparietal.name: Temporoparietal Regions
temporoparietal.function: Critical for phonological processing and reading
temporoparietal.location: Temporal and parietal lobes, above the ear
temporoparietal.findings: Reduced gray matter volume reported, associated with phonological awareness deficits
temporoparietal.significance: Involved in mapping sounds to letters and phonological decoding

grayMatter.note: Replication of gray matter findings has been inconsistent across studies
grayMatter.individualVariability: Individual differences in brain structure are significant, making neuroimaging findings variable across studies

whiteMatter.title: White Matter Connectivity
whiteMatter.overview: Dyslexia is associated with differences in white matter microstructure
whiteMatter.description: White matter consists of myelinated axons that form communication highways between brain regions

arcuateFasciculus.name: Arcuate Fasciculus
arcuateFasciculus.function: Major white matter tract connecting language regions
arcuateFasciculus.pathway: Connects frontal and temporal language areas
arcuateFasciculus.findings: Reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) reported in some studies
arcuateFasciculus.significance: Critical for language processing and reading fluency

perisylvian.name: Left Perisylvian Language Network
perisylvian.significance: Core language network for comprehension and production

visualThalamus.name: Left Visual Thalamus (LGN) to V5/MT
visualThalamus.pathway: From thalamus to motion processing areas
visualThalamus.findings: Reduced structural connectivity in individuals with dyslexia, correlates with rapid naming abilities
visualThalamus.significance: Important for visual processing and rapid naming speed

genetic.title: Genetic Influences on White Matter
genetic.overview: Genetic factors influence white matter connectivity
genetic.finding: READ1 deletion in DCDC2 gene associated with lower global efficiency, local efficiency, and clustering coefficient in white matter networks
genetic.implication: Genetic risk factors affect brain connectivity from early development

functionalActivation.title: Functional Brain Activation
functionalActivation.overview: Functional MRI studies show characteristic activation patterns during reading tasks

patterns.hypoactivation: Hypoactivation in left hemisphere reading networks (occipito-temporal, temporoparietal, inferior frontal regions) - reduced activity in areas critical for reading
patterns.compensatory: Compensatory hyperactivation in right hemisphere homologues in some individuals - right hemisphere attempts to compensate for left hemisphere differences
patterns.connectivity: Altered functional connectivity during reading tasks - different patterns of communication between brain regions

functionalActivation.implications: Activation patterns suggest different neural strategies for reading in individuals with dyslexia

neuralTiming.title: Neural Timing and Oscillations
neuralTiming.overview: Evidence for deficits in neural entrainment and temporal processing
neuralTiming.mechanism: Impaired encoding of low-frequency envelope information (<10Hz, delta and theta band) in speech signal
neuralTiming.theory: Temporal Sampling Theory proposes impaired neural oscillatory entrainment underlies phonological deficits

frequencyBands.gamma: 30+ Hz - related to fine-grained acoustic feature processing

neuralTiming.implications: Neural timing deficits may explain difficulties with speech segmentation and phonological awareness

cerebellum.title: Cerebellar Theory
cerebellum.overview: Cerebellar theory with mixed empirical support
cerebellum.hypothesis: Poor automaticity and motor deficits may be associated with cerebellar dysfunction
cerebellum.location: Located at the base of the brain, traditionally associated with motor coordination
cerebellum.status: Not widely accepted as primary explanation for dyslexia

plasticity.title: Brain Plasticity and Intervention
plasticity.overview: The brain remains plastic throughout life, meaning that intervention can be effective at any age
keyPoints: Neural circuits for reading can be reshaped with intervention
Left hemisphere language areas can show increased activation after training
White matter connectivity can improve with intensive training
The brain's plasticity means outcomes are not fixed
Early intervention is most effective, but adults can also improve reading skills with targeted training

interventionEffects.structural: Changes in gray matter volume with intensive reading intervention
interventionEffects.functional: Normalization of activation patterns in left hemisphere reading networks
interventionEffects.connectivity: Improved white matter connectivity with training

bci.title: Brain-Computer Interface Approaches
bci.finding: Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) approaches show potential for improving phonological processing in developmental dyslexia
bci.status: Experimental, promising but not yet clinically validated

neuroimagingClassification.title: Neuroimaging for Classification
neuroimagingClassification.overview: Machine learning approaches using neuroimaging data
neuroimagingClassification.accuracy: Classification accuracy of 65-90% in controlled cohorts
neuroimagingClassification.caution: Should not be confused with clinical diagnostic utility
neuroimagingClassification.future: May eventually contribute to personalized intervention approaches

sections.name: Developmental Trajectories
sections.description: How dyslexia manifests across the lifespan with maturational asynchrony framework

content.overview: Dyslexia manifests differently across developmental stages. The developmental timing framework proposes that learning disabilities emerge from maturational asynchrony among interacting neural, cognitive, linguistic, sensorimotor, and executive systems rather than from isolated deficits within a single domain. Early identification and intervention can significantly improve outcomes, but the brain remains plastic throughout life.

maturationalAsynchrony.title: Developmental Timing Framework
maturationalAsynchrony.description: Learning disabilities emerge from maturational asynchrony among interacting systems
maturationalAsynchrony.implication: Deficits are not isolated to a single domain but arise from asynchronous development across multiple interacting systems
maturationalAsynchrony.practical: This framework suggests interventions should target multiple domains rather than focusing on a single deficit

longitudinalSubtypes.title: Rate-Disabled vs Accuracy-Disabled Subtypes
longitudinalSubtypes.overview: Longitudinal research supports distinct subtypes with different developmental trajectories

preschool.accuracyDisabled: Deficits in phonological and morphological awareness but intact RAN
preschool.rateDisabled: Impaired RAN but preserved phonological and morphological awareness

firstGrade.accuracyDisabled: Significantly lower reading accuracy, also slower reading rates (low accuracy limits rate)

longitudinalSubtypes.implication: Supports accuracy-rate subtyping of dyslexia with different intervention needs
longitudinalSubtypes.intervention: Accuracy-disabled may need phonological awareness training; rate-disabled may need fluency-focused interventions

stages.name: Early Childhood (3-5 years)
stages.description: Pre-reading period where risk factors can be identified through screening
stages.action: Early screening and phonological awareness activities
stages.research: Preschool deficits in RAN and phonological awareness predict later reading outcomes

stages.name: Early Elementary (5-7 years)
stages.description: Initial reading instruction period - critical window for intervention
stages.action: Intensive phonics instruction and early intervention
stages.research: Early intervention and remediation are critical for dyslexia outcomes

stages.name: Late Elementary (8-10 years)
stages.description: Reading fluency development period - subtypes become differentiated
stages.research: Subtypes become more differentiated (rate-disabled vs accuracy-disabled)

stages.name: Adolescence (11-18 years)
stages.description: Academic demands increase - secondary consequences emerge
stages.research: Secondary consequences include psychological well-being and self-esteem challenges

stages.name: Adulthood (18+ years)
stages.description: Workplace and daily life impact - brain remains plastic
stages.action: Workplace accommodations, assistive technology, adult interventions
stages.research: Employment opportunities may be affected; brain remains plastic for intervention

plasticity.title: Lifelong Brain Plasticity
plasticity.overview: The brain remains plastic throughout life
plasticity.implication: Intervention can be effective at any age, though early intervention is most effective
keyPoints: Neural circuits can be reshaped with intervention at any age
Adults can improve reading skills with targeted training
Motivation and relevance enhance plasticity in adulthood
Different intervention approaches may be needed for different ages

optimizing.early: Early intervention is most efficient due to heightened neural plasticity
optimizing.adult: Adult interventions require more intensive, targeted approaches but can still be effective
optimizing.factors: Motivation, practice intensity, and individualized approach enhance outcomes

researchStats.claims: Part of Phase 3 (10) and Phase 4 (11) claims

sections.name: Manifestations
sections.description: Cognitive, academic, psychological, and social manifestations from 10 verified research claims

content.overview: Dyslexia affects reading, spelling, and related language skills at the word-reading level, with primary difficulties in phonological awareness, decoding, encoding, and/or oral reading fluency. Secondary consequences include psychological well-being and employment opportunities that may be affected. Manifestations vary across individuals and developmental stages.

primary.title: Primary Characteristics
primary.wordLevel: Primary difficulties at the word-reading level
skills: Difficulty with accurate and fluent word recognition
primary.distinction: Distinct from developmental language disorder (DLD) which affects language comprehension, semantics, syntax, and written expression

workingMemory.overview: Children with reading disabilities show deficits in working memory
workingMemory.specific: Particularly pronounced in verbal working memory compared to typically developing peers
workingMemory.metaAnalysis: Meta-analysis highlights that children with RD exhibit significant impairments in working memory, correlating with poor reading comprehension

attention.overview: Children with reading disabilities exhibit deficits in sustained attention and behavioral inhibition
attention.severity: These deficits are typically less severe than those observed in children with ADHD
attention.link: Deficits linked to difficulties in word reading and fluency as attention and inhibition support phonological processing and rapid naming

maturationalAsynchrony.overview: Learning disabilities can emerge from maturational asynchrony among interacting systems
maturationalAsynchrony.implication: Rather than from isolated deficits within a single domain

subtypes.title: Dyslexia Subtypes
subtypes.longitudinal: Preschool deficits predict first-grade reading outcomes, supporting distinct subtypes

biliteracy.title: Biliteracy Manifestations
biliteracy.overview: In bilingual children, distinct biliteracy difficulty subtypes exist
biliteracy.dissociative: Difficulties in one language but not the other (dissociative subtype)
biliteracy.chineseEnglish: Study of Chinese-English children: 57% of Grade 5 children with Chinese reading difficulties did not suffer from English reading difficulties
biliteracy.debate: Whether word reading difficulties are linguistically universal or specific remains debatable

environmentalRiskFactors.overview: Most important environmental risk factors for dyslexia

sections.name: Theoretical Models
sections.description: Scientific frameworks explaining dyslexia from 11 verified research claims

content.overview: Several theoretical models have been proposed to explain dyslexia, each emphasizing different cognitive and neural mechanisms. Research increasingly supports a multiple-deficit perspective, though the phonological deficit hypothesis remains the most influential. Different models explain different aspects of dyslexia and are not mutually exclusive.

models.name: Phonological Deficit Hypothesis
models.description: Proposes that the cognitive basis of many specific reading difficulties is a phonological deficit, characterized by difficulties in processing and manipulating the sound structure of words and grapheme-phoneme correspondences.
models.evidence: Phonological deficits evident across languages and orthographies, in both children and adults with dyslexia
models.implications: Interventions focus on phonological awareness training and phonics instruction
models.limitations: Does not fully account for all cases, particularly those with intact phonological skills

models.name: Double-Deficit Hypothesis
models.description: Posits that difficulties in phonological awareness (PA) and rapid automatized naming (RAN) represent two distinct causes of reading disability, with slow RAN associated with slow reading, whereas poor PA is characterized by inaccurate reading and spelling.
models.evidence: Longitudinal research supports distinct subtypes with different developmental trajectories
models.implications: Different intervention approaches for different subtypes
models.clinical: RAN tasks should be included in assessment to identify rate-disabled subtype

models.name: Temporal Sampling Theory
models.description: Proposes that infants and children extract a phonological system via automatic sensory-motor learning of a hierarchy of amplitude modulations nested in the amplitude envelope of the speech signal. Impaired encoding of low-frequency envelope information (<10Hz, delta and theta band) underlies phonological deficits in dyslexia.
models.evidence: Explains neural entrainment deficits and temporal processing impairments
models.predictions: Predicts that auditory training targeting temporal processing could improve phonological skills
models.research: Active area of current research, not yet fully validated

models.name: Multiple-Deficit Model
models.description: Proposes that dyslexia typically occurs as a result of multiple deficits rather than a single phonological deficit, and some diagnosed cases show no phonological problems at all. Different combinations of genetic, neural, cognitive, and environmental risk factors contribute to different individual profiles.
models.evidence: Recent studies suggest multiple deficits, sometimes with no phonological problems at all
models.implication: Accounts for heterogeneity in dyslexia profiles
models.assessment: Comprehensive assessment should evaluate multiple cognitive domains
models.intervention: Personalized interventions based on individual deficit profiles

models.name: Cerebellar Theory
models.description: States that poor automaticity and motor deficits in individuals with dyslexia may be associated with a dysfunction of the cerebellum.
models.caution: Not widely accepted as primary explanation
models.focus: Explains motor and automaticity deficits, but not core reading difficulties

crossLinguistic.title: Cross-Linguistic Variations
crossLinguistic.overview: Dyslexia manifests differently across languages due to orthographic depth and writing system characteristics

transparent.manifestation: Less problems with accuracy, become rate-disabled with speed deficits and lack of automaticity

opaque.manifestation: Problems in both accuracy and speed of word reading and spelling
opaque.intervention: Focus on both accuracy and fluency

orthographicDepth.implication: Orthographic depth affects how dyslexia manifests and intervention approaches

biliteracy.title: Biliteracy Research
biliteracy.overview: Studies of bilingual children reveal both associative and dissociative dyslexia subtypes
biliteracy.dissociative: Difficulties in one language but not the other
biliteracy.evidence: 57% of Grade 5 children with Chinese reading difficulties did not suffer from English reading difficulties
biliteracy.implication: Word reading difficulties may be language-specific rather than universal

rateVsAccuracy.overview: Longitudinal research supports distinction between rate-disabled and accuracy-disabled subtypes
rateVsAccuracy.preschool: Preschool deficits in RAN and phonological awareness predict first-grade outcomes
rateVsAccuracy.implication: Different developmental trajectories and intervention needs
rateVsAccuracy.longitudinal: Subtypes remain distinct across development, supporting stable individual differences

developmentalTiming.overview: Developmental timing framework proposes maturational asynchrony among interacting systems
developmentalTiming.implication: Learning disabilities emerge from asynchronous development across multiple systems
developmentalTiming.intervention: Should target multiple domains rather than single deficits

domainRelevance.overview: Domain-relevant accounts propose widespread brain differences differentially impact domains relying on those properties
domainRelevance.mechanism: General processing differences that only affect domains particularly reliant on those properties
domainRelevance.example: Temporal processing deficits affect reading but not necessarily other domains

domainSpecific.overview: Domain-specific accounts point to underactivation or structural differences in specific brain regions
domainSpecific.mechanism: Differences in brain processing systems specific to the domain showing cognitive strength or weakness
domainSpecific.example: Left hemisphere language network differences specific to reading

additive.description: Children with ADHD + RD exhibit more severe deficits in attention, inhibition, working memory, and RAN due to combined impairments
additive.evidence: Supported by additive effects in cognitive profiles
additive.implication: Comorbid cases require integrated intervention approaches

integrativePerspective.title: Integrative Perspective
integrativePerspective.overview: No single model explains all aspects of dyslexia
integrativePerspective.approach: Multiple models are complementary rather than mutually exclusive
integrativePerspective.clinical: Assessment and intervention should consider multiple perspectives
integrativePerspective.future: Research continues to refine our understanding of how these models interact

sections.name: Interventions
sections.description: Evidence-based intervention approaches from Phase 5 research

content.overview: Intervention research for dyslexia includes phonological training, brain-based approaches, environmental interventions, multisensory methods, and technology-based solutions. Early intervention and remediation are critical for dyslexia outcomes. The brain remains plastic throughout life, meaning intervention can be effective at any age.

earlyIntervention.title: Early Intervention
earlyIntervention.overview: Early intervention and remediation are critical for dyslexia outcomes
earlyIntervention.implication: Early identification and intervention significantly improve outcomes
earlyIntervention.plasticity: Brain remains plastic throughout life, allowing for intervention effectiveness at any age
earlyIntervention.criticalWindow: Ages 5-7 represent a critical window for reading development and intervention
earlyIntervention.preschool: Preschool screening can identify risk factors before formal reading instruction begins

phonologicalTraining.title: Phonological Training
phonologicalTraining.overview: Systematic instruction in phonological awareness and phonics
components: Phoneme awareness (identifying and manipulating individual sounds)
phonologicalTraining.effectiveness: Well-established as evidence-based intervention for dyslexia

multisensory.overview: Teaching methods that engage multiple senses simultaneously

ortonGillingham.name: Orton-Gillingham Approach
ortonGillingham.description: Structured, sequential, multisensory approach to teaching reading
ortonGillingham.evidence: Widely used, though empirical support varies by implementation

multisensory.rationale: Engaging multiple senses may strengthen neural pathways for reading

fluencyTraining.title: Reading Fluency Training
fluencyTraining.overview: Approaches to improve reading speed, accuracy, and expression
methods: Repeated reading of the same text
fluencyTraining.outcomes: Improved automaticity and comprehension with fluency gains

assistiveTechnology.overview: Tools that support reading and writing
assistiveTechnology.benefits: Access to content despite reading difficulties, reduces fatigue

bci.title: Brain-Computer Interface Approaches
bci.finding: BCI approaches show potential for improving phonological processing in developmental dyslexia
bci.future: May contribute to personalized neurofeedback interventions

comprehensionStrategies.overview: Strategies to improve understanding of text
comprehensionStrategies.application: Important once basic decoding skills are established

accommodations.overview: Modifications that support access while maintaining standards
educational: Extended time on tests and assignments

sections.name: Controversies & Debates
sections.description: Ongoing debates and unresolved issues in dyslexia research from 20 verified claims

content.overview: Dyslexia research has several ongoing controversies and debates, including assessment criteria, cross-linguistic issues, policy controversies, and neurobiological disagreements. These debates reflect the complexity of dyslexia and the diversity of perspectives in the field.

delphi.overview: Delphi consensus definition (Carroll et al. 2025) has unresolved issues
issues: Lack of clear guidance for educators

iqDiscrepancy.conflict: ICD-11 uses discrepancy criterion relative to age and IQ, while DSM-5-TR focuses on unexpected levels relative to age and educational opportunities
iqDiscrepancy.consensus: No universal scientific consensus regarding role of IQ-achievement discrepancy scores
iqDiscrepancy.metsala: Metsala and colleagues regard discrepancy definition as 'serious error that should be explicitly challenged'

cutoffVsContinuum.continuum: 83% of panelists agreed dyslexic difficulties exist on a continuum
cutoffVsContinuum.cutoff: 65% agreed cut-off criteria are important (below 80% threshold for acceptance)

cognitiveTesting.overview: Role of cognitive testing in assessment
cognitiveTesting.delphi: Delphi consensus supports including elements of cognitive processing
cognitiveTesting.metsala: Metsala et al. disagree with this
cognitiveTesting.morsanyi: Morsanyi et al. argue lack of clear guidance on range of cognitive tests is regrettable

stealthDyslexia.overview: Stealth dyslexia not addressed in definitions
stealthDyslexia.description: Individuals with high cognitive abilities who compensate for dyslexia may not meet criteria despite underlying phonological difficulties

unexpectedness.criticism: Defining dyslexia in terms of unexpectedness may be inequitable for economically disadvantaged children
unexpectedness.ida2025: IDA 2025 removed unexpectedness language to address this concern

universality.overview: Whether word reading difficulties are linguistically universal or specific
universality.lcdh: Linguistic Coding Difference Hypothesis suggests difficulty in one language implies difficulty in another
universality.alternative: Alternative perspective allows for difficulty in one language but not another
universality.evidence: Studies show both associative (both languages) and dissociative (one language) subtypes

biliteracy.finding: 57% of Grade 5 children with Chinese reading difficulties did not suffer from English reading difficulties
biliteracy.implication: Evidence supports both universal and specific perspectives

policy.overview: Debates about educational policy, screening practices, and resource allocation
policy.implications: Different definitions and criteria affect policy decisions and resource distribution

sections.name: Research Methodology
sections.description: Research design, measurement, and statistical analysis methods from 14 verified claims

content.overview: Dyslexia research employs diverse methodologies including genetic studies (GWAS), neuroimaging, cognitive assessments, and longitudinal designs. Methodological rigor is essential for valid conclusions, with attention to research design, measurement validity, and appropriate statistical analysis.
